headline: US economy sheds 23,000 jobs, markets rally on Fed rate cut hopes
tldr: US July jobs report missed by 106,000; Wall Street rallied with S&P up 0.5% and Nasdaq up 1.1%.
Bank of England held rates at 3.75% in July; UK is in its longest jobs slump since the financial crisis.
Iran's parliament is reviewing a plan to ban US and Israeli-linked ships from the Strait of Hormuz, threatening global oil flows.
Motor insurance market forecast to worsen in 2026 with a combined ratio of 108%; premiums expected to rise 4% this year.
MK Tech Week runs 12–16 October, with a sovereign technology conference at Unity Place on 15 October.

sections.title: Markets
sections.body:
**Markets — Friday 7 August 2026**

The dominant story today is the US July jobs report. 
The economy lost 23,000 jobs in July, against a consensus expectation of +83,000 gains.
 That's a sharp miss — and markets treated it as good news. 
Wall Street bet that signs of a weakening labour market increase the chances of a Fed rate cut,
 reversing Thursday's gloom. 
The S&P 500 gained around 0.5% and the Nasdaq rose 1.1%.
 
The 10-year Treasury yield fell five basis points to 4.63%
 as bond markets priced in less pressure on the Fed to hike.

The Fed backdrop matters here. 
The FOMC held rates at 3.50–3.75% for a fifth straight meeting in July, though three members dissented in favour of a 25bp hike — leaving a September move live.
 
Core PCE has accelerated to 3.3%,
 which is why today's jobs softness shifts the balance: it reduces the hawkish case.

Thursday had been weaker. 
The S&P fell 0.18% as traders weighed Middle East uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz and mixed corporate earnings.
 
AppLovin tumbled nearly 20% on mixed results, and Western Digital shed 13% on a disappointing first-quarter forecast.


In Europe, 
European shares closed at a record high for a third straight session on Thursday — the STOXX 600 adding 0.2% — as investors assessed progress toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz alongside positive earnings.
 
The FTSE 100 closed Thursday at 10,867.89, down 0.2%, and opened Friday broadly flat.
 
The FTSE was separately boosted by a metals rally this morning.


**Sam's portfolio — notable movers**

- **BAE Systems +2.04%** — the standout, likely riding continued defence spending optimism. Rolls-Royce gave back 2.36%, no obvious single catalyst beyond profit-taking after a strong run.
- **ASML +1.56%, AMD +1.50%** — tech bouncing with the Nasdaq. AMD reported earnings earlier this week; 
AMD earnings featured on 4 August as part of the record-setting tech comeback.

- 
Brent crude strengthened to $83.71 a barrel this morning,
 which supports energy-exposed names but adds inflationary risk — watch Brent closely given the Strait of Hormuz negotiations still in flux. 
Oil is wavering as traders weigh those negotiations.

**Gameweek 1 — Deadline: Friday 21 Aug, 18:30 BST**

Prices are locked until the deadline passes. 
All prices will remain frozen until the GW1 deadline on 21 August at 18:30 BST
, so no price rises or falls to chase yet — focus your energy on squad construction rather than the transfer market.

**Injuries & doubts to know**

Based on the pre-fetched flagged players data:

- **Kroupi Jr (Bournemouth, £4.7m, 4.7% owned)** — foot injury, no return date. 
He is among the clearest current avoids
 for GW1.
- **Šeško (Man Utd, £?, 2.7% owned)** — shin injury, 75% chance of playing. 
A 75% flag doesn't mean the player will start or complete 90 minutes — it only signals participation is considered more likely than not.

- **Tielemans & Lisandro Martínez (Man Utd)** — both carrying injuries at 75% likelihood. Worth waiting for the pre-match press conference before committing.
- **Jakub Kiwior / J. Timber (Arsenal, £6.5m)** — groin injury, expected back 21 Aug. That's cutting it very fine for the deadline; treat as doubtful.
- **Garner (Everton)** — groin, expected back 22 Aug — after the deadline. Avoid.

**New for 2026/27: Price Change Predictor**


A new level of transparency on player price changes is being added from GW1, with the daily price change deadline set at midnight UK time.
 
The tool will help managers identify players who could be close to rising or falling, reducing the risk of being priced out of a planned transfer.


**Premium prices to note**


Haaland carries a record price of £15.5m, while Bruno Fernandes has received the joint-biggest price rise from last season, up £3.0m to £12.0m.


**Standout differential angle**


The highest-value uncertainty heading into GW1 is Arsenal's £5.5m defender slot
 — with Timber's fitness unclear and Saliba also absent, there's rotation risk across their backline despite Arsenal otherwise being heavily represented in popular squads.

sections.title: Data & BI
sections.body:
**Data & BI** · 7 August 2026

**Power BI — July update now live**


The July 2026 Power BI release adds capabilities across reporting, modelling, mobile, and embedded analytics. Key highlights include expanded modern visual defaults, conditional formatting for line charts and legends, model options in the service, and TMDL View on the web.


A few items worth actioning:

- **Report-wide theming is finally centralised.** 
The modern visual defaults preview now includes a "Customize current theme" experience directly in the Format pane, letting you adjust report-wide defaults that apply to all visuals — without manually styling each one.

- **Measure docs in code.** 
You can now write measure descriptions via triple-slash comments right where you define the measure
 — a small but genuinely useful quality-of-life change for larger models.
- **Settings pane rollout.** 
Starting in August, semantic model settings in the Power BI Service open in the new settings pane rather than the full settings page.

- **OneDrive/SharePoint deadline.** 
From October, users on Power BI Desktop versions from March 2026 or earlier will no longer be able to save and share files to OneDrive and SharePoint.
 Worth flagging to any teams slow on updates.

**BigQuery — continuous queries reach GA**


BigQuery's continuous queries have reached general availability. Any data written to a table — via Storage Write API, streaming, batch load, or INSERT — can now be pushed to a new BigQuery table, a Pub/Sub topic, or Bigtable in real time.
 This removes a meaningful gap versus Snowflake Dynamic Tables for event-driven pipelines. Separately, 
BigQuery Graph is now available in preview, offering a scalable graph analytics solution for modelling and analysing massive-scale relationships.


**Semantic layer — AI is the forcing function**


Semantic layers stopped being a BI accessory in 2026: AI agents now answer business questions directly, and they need governed metrics — not raw tables — to answer consistently.
 The practical implication: 
AI analytics failures are more often semantic failures than hallucinations — the model picks the wrong table, joins at the wrong grain, or aggregates incorrectly. A governed semantic layer prevents the majority of these errors before a query is ever run.


On the dbt side, 
MetricFlow resolves metric names to SQL with grain validation, and invalid dimension combinations fail at compile time — a critical guardrail for AI agents that might otherwise invent joins.
 Teams not yet using MetricFlow should treat AI agent ambitions as the business case to start.

sections.title: Career & Data Leadership
sections.body:
**Career & Data Leadership** · 7 August 2026

**Market conditions**


Demand for UK data professionals is up 7.7% year-on-year for new postings
, so the market is growing even if it is not uniformly buoyant. 
Data analysts and AI engineers are holding up because businesses continue to invest in automation and insight capabilities
 — but 
the wider tech and data jobs market remains challenging, with some organisations slowing hiring, rationalising projects, or merging data teams with software or analytics functions.


**Salary benchmarks**


Head of Data or data management leadership roles frequently exceed £90,000, particularly where responsibility includes governance, reporting strategy, and enterprise data architecture oversight.
 Across the broader data discipline, 
salaries are rising by 2–4% on average, with stronger growth of up to 6% in AI, data, and cybersecurity.
 On geography: 
remote working has compressed but not eliminated the London premium — London roles pay roughly 20–30% more than equivalent roles in Manchester, Leeds, and Birmingham, but purchasing power is broadly equivalent.
 Worth bearing in mind for any role that comes up outside the capital.

**What's shaping senior hiring**


Organisations are increasingly looking for leaders who can influence enterprise-wide transformation spanning product, data, technology, and customer strategy — leadership hires prioritise versatility over narrow specialist expertise.
 The specific ask at Head/Director level is AI literacy baked in: 
there is a distinct scarcity of digital expertise, resulting in sharply rising and highly competitive salaries, particularly for leadership roles in AI, Cloud, and Data.
 
66% of data specialists say they are open to new opportunities this year
 — useful context both for your own positioning and for the retention risk you'd inherit as a new leader.

**Leadership lens**

The sharpest challenge flagged by practitioners right now is visibility, not capability. 
In 2026, the defining risk for data leaders is that technical credibility is no longer sufficient — the executives driving real impact are those who lead the business *through* data, not just lead the data function.
 Tactically, 
the differentiator will not be what analytics teams can build, but what they can deliver, communicate, and make stick — organisations that treat project management as a strategic capability, not an afterthought, will win out.

sections.title: UK Insurance
sections.body:
**UK Insurance**

**FCA regulatory posture**


The FCA published its first annual Regulatory Priorities report for the insurance sector in February 2026. It replaces the previous portfolio letter format and is designed to give all UK insurers a clearer, more predictable view of supervisory intent.
 
The four stated priorities are: improving consumer understanding, claims handling and service quality; increasing access to insurance; ensuring fair value under Consumer Duty; and strengthening operational resilience.


On Consumer Duty specifically, 
the FCA is leaning more heavily on the Duty rather than introducing new product-specific rules, and will consult on further simplification including GAP insurance rules, general insurance pricing data, and information disclosure requirements.



Premium finance remains under watch: whilst the FCA notes cost reductions since 2022, it will continue to monitor APRs and act where fair value concerns persist.



The FCA has also flagged pet and private medical insurance for monitoring, having identified price increases and consumer understanding issues in both.


**Motor market**


Following a profitable 2024 (NCR 98%), the motor market fell back into the red in 2025 with an estimated NCR of 102%, and greater losses are forecast for 2026 at 108% — driven primarily by premium rate reductions since late 2024 feeding through to earned premium, alongside continued claims inflation.



After premiums fell by almost 12% during 2025, EY expects motor insurance premiums to increase by 4% in 2026 and a further 12% in 2027 as insurers respond to continued claims cost pressure.
 
The end of the softening cycle, combined with increasing divergence in pricing decisions between carriers, is likely to intensify price sensitivity at renewal and generate Consumer Duty compliance scrutiny as some insurers move sharply whilst others hold.


**MGA / insurtech**


The MGAA 2026 conference signalled a market shifting away from AI experimentation and towards responsible deployment, with governance, accountability, and decision intelligence emerging as central themes.
 
Separately, the FCA's focus on proving good customer outcomes is actively shifting insurers' AI priorities from adoption to governance
 — a practical constraint on how quickly AI tooling can be embedded into pricing and underwriting workflows.

sections.title: Milton Keynes
sections.body:
**Events — diary these**

- **📅 4 Aug (Mon, this week — already passed)** — [Code For Her](https://protospace.uk/events) meetup at Aiimi HQ, 18:30–20:30. Worth watching for next month's date.
- **📅 27 Aug (Thu)** — 
MKFM's Meet of MK End of Summer Party at Hotel La Tour, from 5pm.
 Broad professional crowd; good for cross-sector contacts.
- **📅 10 Sep (Thu)** — 
MKC TV in partnership with Work Café Santander at Unity Place, from 5:30pm.

- **📅 12–16 Oct** — **MK Tech Week.** 
Building on last year's success, which saw more than 23,000 people attend 30+ events.
 
The centrepiece conference focuses on sovereign technology — the UK's ability to develop, secure and control critical technologies and digital infrastructure — with a one-day conference and expo at Unity Place on **15 October.**
 
Highlights also include The Future of Adult and Lifelong Learning in the Age of AI at The Open University, and Stadium MK's Stadiums of the Future showcase.
 Register interest now at miltonkeynestechweek.com.

**Local news**

- **Oxford–MK rail row.** 
The billion-pound Oxford–MK line, which has left passengers waiting two years, could finally open by end of 2026, with rail minister Lord Peter Hendy indicating services are timetabled.
 However, 
Chiltern Railways has been locked in dispute with the RMT union since 2024 over driver-only operation plans — the union insists a guard must be present on trains making the 42-minute MK–Oxford run.
 A fresh complication to watch.
- **Council politics.** 
Following May's elections, the council is under no overall control with the Lib Dems the largest party; a Lib Dem–Labour alliance has formed, led by Cllr Jane Carr.

- **Roads.** 
MK roads are receiving a £6m maintenance boost, with 11 roads earmarked for resurfacing.

- **Coach connectivity.** 
The council is championing growth of the FlixBus coach service for residents and visitors.

- **Schools.** 
Stantonbury School has been placed in special measures following an Ofsted inspection.

sections.title: News
sections.body:
I was able to find solid confirmed stories from today's date (7 August 2026) from Just Security, NPR, and Bloomberg/Commons Library. Here is the News section, drawing only on what the searches actually confirmed.

---

**🗞 News**

**UK economy**


The Bank of England held interest rates at 3.75% at its 30 July MPC meeting — rates have been cut by 1.5 percentage points in total since August 2024.
 The labour market remains a drag: 
Bloomberg notes the UK is in its longest jobs slump since the financial crisis, per PMI data.
 On the fiscal side, 
Chancellor John Healey has confirmed the first Budget will be delivered on 28 October.


**Yemen / Middle East**


Houthi rebels attacked Yemeni military positions in Marib and Hadramout provinces, killing at least 30 military personnel according to Yemen's state news agency.
 
Hours later, Saudi Arabia reported that separate Houthi strikes wounded more than 10 civilians in the southern Najran region, near the Yemeni border.


**Strait of Hormuz**


Iran's parliament is reviewing a plan to ban ships linked to the US, Israel and other "hostile countries" from transiting the Strait of Hormuz
 — a move that would directly threaten global oil flows if passed.

**Thailand school shooting**


A shooting at a school in Thailand's Nonthaburi province today left deaths and injuries; the shooter was a student.
 Motive is still under investigation.

**Sudan humanitarian crisis**


Hundreds of thousands of civilians in el-Obeid are being battered by relentless drone strikes and face critical water shortages and a worsening cholera outbreak, while women and girls are reporting high rates of sexual violence.
